We identify challenges in adapting interfaces while preserving continuity, coordinating attention across tasks, providing responsive interaction, and learning user habits over time. The aim is to support continuing task control while protecting attention for primary work.

papers.title: Beyond Classical Minimax Rates: Quantum Sampling in Gradient-Based Simulation Optimization
papers.summary: We study gradient-based search for a class of convex simulation optimization problems with gradients estimated from noisy outputs. With independent outputs, the optimal classical convergence rate for the expected objective gap is of order $O(N^{-2/3})$, where $N$ is the query budget. We apply quantum mean estimation to paired finite differences and progressively increase their estimation accuracy as the perturbations shrink, improving the convergence rate to $O(N^{-4/3})$. Furthermore, we show that coupling nearby evaluations improves the classical and quantum convergence rates to $O(N^{-2/(3-κ)})$ and $O(N^{-4/(3-κ)})$, respectively, where $κ\in[0,1]$ describes the variance reduction in paired outputs. Thus, quantum estimation halves the accuracy exponent in query complexity across coupling orders. Moreover, we establish matching lower bounds and show that these accuracy exponents are minimax optimal for fixed decision dimension, even when query locations and batch sizes are adaptive. Reconstruction from feasible differences retains the exponents when every simulation query must be feasible and accommodates boundary optima.

papers.title: Completing the real-space construction of the canonical harmonic coordinates of Kerr metric
papers.summary: In this paper, we determine the exact canonical harmonic Kerr metric to all post-Minkowskian (PM) orders within the multipolar post-Minkowskian (MPM) formalism. The metric agrees with the previously constructed 4PM results. Using a formal series ring, we prove that no homogeneous components of Laplacian operator appear in this metric at PM order $n\ge2$. Together with the equality of the linear field with the canonical Kerr solution, this property allows an inductive construction of the canonical MPM metric where all gauge moments vanish. The coordinate transformation linking the canonical harmonic Kerr metric to the Boyer-Lindquist metric is generated by the real part of a complex harmonic radial function. A recent independent construction by Sadu and Vanhove using momentum-space recursion and a residual homogeneous freedom classification yields the same result, providing a cross validation of the closed-form canonical harmonic Kerr metric.

papers.title: Not Just Any Example: Security Requirements and Fix Patterns for Guiding LLM Vulnerability Repair
papers.summary: Software vulnerabilities leave systems open to attack, and their remediation is often delayed. Large language models (LLMs) have advanced automated patch generation, yet passing functionality tests does not ensure that a patch enforces the security requirement the vulnerability violated. Existing vulnerability repair techniques rely on curated patterns or templates with limited coverage, leaving unclear which repair strategies carry over across vulnerabilities and how they can steer LLMs. We present a large-scale empirical study that relates recurring fix patterns to the security impacts of vulnerabilities and examines how this knowledge can guide LLM-based repair. Building on a manual study of security patches, we cluster 3,816 security patches from 348 open-source repositories and analyze the edits and their context to derive concrete fix patterns, ranging from local safeguards to coordinated changes across multiple locations. We define 12 security impact classes by the security requirements that vulnerabilities violate and map them to repair categories and fix patterns, revealing characteristic repairs, alternative strategies within a class, and patterns shared across classes. We then use these patterns and impact-pattern associations to select repair examples for four LLMs on repair tasks of varying complexity. Guided example selection raises the four-model mean pass@3 from 37.9% under zero-shot prompting to up to 49.2%, whereas randomly selected examples reach only 36.9%. Our findings connect vulnerability characterization with patch generation and support organizing repair knowledge around security requirements.

papers.title: Audits Need Access, Data, and Compute. But How Much?
papers.summary: AI audits have garnered significant attention in recent months, as the ability to test and monitor AI models plays a crucial role in safe development and deployment. However, AI audit success hinges on an auditor's authority; in particular, what information and resources they have at their disposal. Ongoing debates have surrounded the question: How much model access is needed to conduct an AI audit? Auditors seek more model access, while companies resist it for reasons related to confidential business information (trade secrets) and privacy. This tug-of-war remains unresolved. Further, this debate misses a related question: How much data and compute do auditors need? In this work, we systematically investigate both questions. We provide a framework that varies each of these three dimensions-model access, data, and compute-and measures their joint effect on audit success. We apply this framework to three tasks. We find that (1) some model access is important, but there can be diminishing returns; (2) data and compute matter more for traditional fairness audits, but model access matters more for manipulation and lie detection; and (3) these three resources can be fungible (i.e., an exchange rate exists between them), meaning that model access is not the only salient factor. These results suggest that audit governance should jointly consider different dimensions of auditor authority (including model access, data, and compute) in relation to audit objectives. These issues are particularly salient as we consider the spectrum of auditing setups, from a small ecosystem of embedded evaluators with significant access to a large body of third-party auditors with greater independence but limited access. Our framework serves as a template that can be applied to different audit tasks and inform the degree of auditor authority.

papers.title: Are Web Agents Still Detectable? Stress-Testing Bot Defenses with Coordinated Evasion
papers.summary: AI web agents can autonomously navigate websites and complete various tasks. As their capabilities and adoption expand, evaluating bot defenses requires adversarial stress tests. Although prior work demonstrates that existing agents can remain detectable, it remains unclear how effective bot defenses are against adversaries that coordinate evasion across browser fingerprints, automation controls, and interaction behavior. To investigate this threat, we introduce DarkAgent, an autonomous web agent that combines a forked Chromium browser that conceals automation artifacts and generative models that produce human-like mouse and keyboard traces. To address the limitations of existing keyboard mimickers, our keyboard model jointly generates realistic key events and their timings while reliably reproducing the target text. Released agent detectors accept our generated behavior as human, and trained classifiers find it substantially harder to distinguish from human traces than existing mimickers. DarkAgent achieves an 89% page-access bypass rate across a third-party stealth benchmark, exceeding the strongest published baseline by 12 percentage points. To further enhance the measurement of agents, we introduce a benchmark that measures browser fingerprints, interaction behavior, and network activity to assess each channel's contribution to detecting adversarial agents such as DarkAgent. On this benchmark, browser and behavioral modifications are complementary: either alone remains detectable, and only their combination evades all tested checks. Together, our findings expose the gap between passing existing bot defenses and reproducing human behavior, and point to timing between actions as a remaining signal for defenders.

papers.title: Beyond "AI Can Make Mistakes": How Risk Communication Shapes Trust and Decision Confidence for LLMs in Health Information Seeking
papers.summary: Adoption of LLMs for health information has outpaced public understanding, but whether risk communication can work as a corrective remains unknown. In a preregistered experiment (N=500), we compared a standard disclaimer against structured risk communication varying in contextual relevance and mechanistic explanation. Without intervention, users understanding LLMs less reported higher trust and confidence in deciding when to rely. Structured risk communication significantly reduced trust, more so with health-specific framing, but did not improve confidence in reliance decision. Risk disclosure was associated with higher decision confidence among those with stronger AI knowledge, but lower confidence among those less preferring analytical thinking. Effects were also task-dependent: disclosure shifted preferences for medical queries and impairment assistance, while LLMs remained preferred for emotional companionship regardless of exposure. These findings demonstrate that risk communication can narrow trust gaps across AI-literacy levels, but turning disclosure into judgment requires adapting to usage context and users' prior knowledge.

papers.title: Machine learning enables full Bayesian inference for spinning extreme-mass-ratio inspirals
papers.summary: Extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs), stellar-mass compact objects spiralling into massive black holes, promise to measure the masses and spins of the central black holes, reveal the strong-field environment around them and gauge cosmic distances via millihertz gravitational-wave observations. Yet most forecasts for the parameter inference of these systems assume known source parameters, and broad-prior analyses have addressed only simplified versions of the problem. The joint inversion of all 14 parameters of a spinning source from the complete prior has remained unsolved. Here we solve it for the augmented analytic kludge model: generative networks narrow the complete prior and reveal a ring of degenerate spin directions, and the exact detector likelihood determines the posterior. For a simulated one-year LISA-Taiji observation, within one ring sector we obtain, for the first time, a 14-parameter posterior of a spinning EMRI from the complete prior, the most precise yet obtained for such a source from broad priors. The redshifted mass and spin of the massive black hole are determined to two parts in $10^5$, the mass two orders of magnitude beyond any electromagnetic measurement. The compact object's redshifted mass is measured to one part in $10^4$, and its eccentric, retrograde orbit discriminates between capture channels. The 0.8% distance and sub-square-degree localization are sufficient for dark-siren cosmology. Year-long coherent analysis resolves the inspiral driven by radiation reaction itself.
papers.comment: 22 pages, 5 figures, 1 table; Extended Data: 4 figures, 2 tables

papers.title: Meta-Amortized Cognitive Modeling
papers.summary: Cognitive modeling is highly iterative. Researchers repeatedly revise model structures, parameterizations, covariates, and experimental designs as theories evolve and data accumulates. Amortized Bayesian inference with neural networks provides rapid estimation for individual models, but every revision requires new simulations and training. Here, we introduce CogFormerV2, a meta-amortized framework that enables researchers to specify, revise, and fit cognitive models with a single network, carrying amortization across an entire space of models all at once. Trained once in about a day on a single GPU, it delivers accurate, well-calibrated posteriors across more than 14.6 billion model configurations spanning binary, multi-alternative, and continuous decisions, with varying parameter sets, covariate structures, trial counts, and contamination levels. It can fit empirical data from distinct behavioral tasks and extends to new models through continual learning and representation transfer. Released as an open-source interactive application, CogFormerV2 provides a reusable infrastructure for meta-amortized inference in cognitive modeling, while carrying the potential to accelerate computational modeling workflows at large.

papers.title: Classical phase space distributions for quantum states in cosmology: General states, operator ordering and the geometry of fading non-commutativity
papers.summary: In earlier work with Ashtekar and Kesavan we showed that, for linear fields in any FLRW background, the vacuum defines a probability distribution $ρ_o$ on the classical phase space whose moments are exactly the Weyl-ordered $n$-point functions. We extend that analysis in four directions. First, for an arbitrary state $Ψ$ we give an explicit formula, in the Bargmann representation, for the distribution $ρ_Ψ$ that reproduces all Weyl-ordered expectation values. For pure states it is non-negative precisely for coherent and squeezed states, each the Gaussian of a compatible Kähler metric, and the Gaussian smoothing needed to make it positive is either zero or the full coherent-state width. Second, for linear observables every operator ordering differs from the Weyl ordering by explicit products of $c$-number commutators. Third, for two linear observables in a pure Gaussian state, the classical correlation coefficient, the ratio of commutator to anticommutator and the squeezing are functions of a single angle between their Hamiltonian vector fields; this bounds the departure of arbitrarily ordered $n$-point functions from the moments of $ρ$. Fourth, for fields in FLRW the equality holds at arbitrary, possibly different, times and for every homogeneous isotropic quasi-free state. In de Sitter the non-commutative corrections fall as $e^{-N}$ for field and momentum and as $e^{-3N}/3$ for the field at two times. For the state inherited from inflation they stay suppressed in the radiation era, by the inverse occupation number, except near the nodes of the mode functions. The same squeezing entangles the modes $\pm\vec k$ relative to the radiation-era vacuum and makes displaced-parity measurements violate Bell inequalities, so the positive distribution describes a specified family of observables, not all measurements.

papers.title: A General Framework for Identifying the Joint Potential Outcome Distribution through Support Restrictions
papers.summary: Many causal estimands depend on the joint distribution of potential outcomes, which is generally not identifiable because only one potential outcome can be observed for each unit. To obtain identification, researchers often impose assumptions such as monotonicity and exclusion restriction that constrain the support of this joint distribution. For treatments and outcomes that each take finitely many values, we define a similarity matrix whose entries count, for each pair of potential outcome strata, the number of treatments yielding the same outcome. We then prove that, under unconfoundedness, identification holds if and only if this matrix is invertible, yielding a criterion directly verifiable from the support. In addition, we derive an identification formula for the joint distribution under these support restrictions and show that an average causal estimand is identifiable if and only if its integrand admits an additive representation on the restricted support. Finally, we derive sharp testable implications of the support restriction. Our results unify and generalize a broad range of identification results in the literature.

papers.title: Beyond Average Gains: Probing the Equity--Vulnerability Tension in Structured Visual AI for Learning
papers.summary: Open-ended conversational AI requires learners to formulate questions, organize learning paths, and track changing problem states. Structured visual interfaces may ease these demands, but higher average ratings do not establish that support is experienced consistently across learner backgrounds and devices. We conducted a randomized study of graph-algorithm learning, comparing VisualCodeChat (VCC), which combines predefined learning stages, conversational explanations, and dynamic algorithm visualizations, with a standard text-based chatbot. We analyzed 282 post-task questionnaires from university students. In unadjusted comparisons, VCC received significantly higher usability and perceived effectiveness ratings. We detected no significant between-condition differences in efficiency, satisfaction, or post-use emotion. Exploratory within-condition analyses identified differences associated with prior chatbot experience: infrequent users reported lower adoption and learning-management ratings in the standard AI condition, while uncomfortable prior chatbot experiences were associated with lower interaction and layout ratings in the VCC condition. These findings suggest that improving the average interaction experience is only part of making AI-supported learning inclusive. Future evaluations should examine whether learners with different prior experiences can obtain guidance, recover from difficulties, and demonstrate understanding independently across devices.

papers.title: A General Framework for E-process Stopping Rules in Best-Arm Identification
papers.summary: We propose an e-process stopping rule in the best-arm identification problem. The e-process stopping rule is different from the Chernoff stopping rule by its hypothesis structure on the stopping decision. The major benefit of an e-process stopping rule is the flexibility in stopping rule design and in fact, it recovers previously suggested Chernoff stopping rule on several bandit problems. Moreover, we analyze the asymptotic optimality of the $δ$-PAC algorithm with the decomposition of e-processes. The decomposition separates optimality conditions into three parts; the sampling policy allocation convergence, the efficiency of e-process design, and the bandit problem's inherent stochastic behavior. Subsequently, we prove a sufficient condition for asymptotic optimality in bandit algorithms. For the application of an e-process stopping rule, we derived an asymptotically optimal algorithm for the generalized linear bandit problem.

papers.title: The Effect of Remote Working on Regional Waste: Evidence from South Korea
papers.summary: Remote working, or work-from-home (WFH), has become common around the world. However, its broader effects on social welfare, including waste generation, remain understudied. This study examines the impact of remote work on regional waste production in South Korea, using the COVID-19 pandemic as a natural experiment. Overall household waste changed little, but regions with greater WFH eligibility saw increases in plastic and textile waste and a decrease in food waste. These findings suggest that remote work may change consumption patterns and daily routines. Understanding these effects can help inform sustainable work practices and waste management as remote work becomes more widespread.

papers.title: Prospects for Detecting Post-merger Signals from Binary Neutron Stars with Future Gravitational-Wave Detectors
papers.summary: The post-merger (PM) phase of binary neutron star (BNS) mergers carries information about the merger remnant and the dense-matter equation of state, but its observational prospects remain uncertain. We compare two approaches to accessing this emission: the stochastic gravitational-wave background (SGWB) from the BNS population and direct PM-band detections of individually resolved mergers. Using a unified inspiral--merger--post-merger (IPM) waveform prescription and the same astrophysical population model for both calculations, we evaluate representative third-generation detector configurations involving ET, CE, and a dedicated kilohertz detector. For the representative detector networks considered, the baseline IPM model predicts that the all-source, broadband BNS SGWB exceeds the adopted detection threshold across the local merger-rate interval. In contrast, the kilohertz PM-band SGWB remains below this threshold. For individual events, over $R_0=7.6$--$250~{\rm Gpc}^{-3}\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$, the baseline IPM model predicts approximately $5$--$174$ PM-band candidates per year for the dedicated kilohertz detector, whereas the numerical-relativity cases considered here yield approximately $0.07$--$7~{\rm yr}^{-1}$.
papers.comment: Accepted for publication in Chinese Physics C

papers.title: Background characterization in the PIKACHU Phase 1 search for two-neutrino double-beta decay of $^{160}$Gd
papers.summary:
We report a background characterization for the search for two-neutrino double-beta ($2
u2β$) decay of $^{160}$Gd using Ce:Gd$_3$Al$_2$Ga$_3$O$_{12}$ scintillators in the PIKACHU experiment Phase 1 at the Kamioka underground laboratory. The experimental backgrounds were investigated through delayed-coincidence analysis and spectral fitting based on GEANT4 simulations. In particular, surface contamination of the crystal was identified through the characteristic distortion of the $^{214}$Po $α$-ray spectrum, leading to an improved background model that reproduces the observed energy spectra. No significant excess attributable to $^{160}$Gd $2
u2β$ decay was observed, yielding a lower limit of $T^{2ν}_{1/2} \geq 2.32 	imes 10^{19}$ yr at 90\% C.L. The established background model and analysis framework provide a foundation for future PIKACHU phases aiming to discover $^{160}$Gd $2
u2β$ decay.

papers.title: Not All Interpretation Methods Are Created Equal: Tiered Evaluation of AI Interpretability
papers.summary: As AI transitions to sociotechnical deployments, uninterpretable models pose serious threats to reliability, public trust and contestability. However, not all interpretation methods are created equal: for interpretability to enhance deployment safety and effectiveness, interpretation methods must be evaluated in a tiered system to differentiate evidence levels of trustworthiness, rather than validated through isolated interpretation instances. Our core vision is that elevating the evaluation of interpretation methods to a core AI assessment metric will drive robust knowledge discovery from data (KDD) and ensure safe, contestable sociotechnical deployments of AI. To this end, we propose TRUST, a tiered evaluation framework that builds upon the Predictability-Computability-Stability (PCS) principles for Veridical Data Science (VDS) and the Predictive, Descriptive and Relevant (PDR) foundations. To differentiate interpretation methods effectively and systematically, TRUST grades interpretation across five tiers: Task-Aligned PDR Foundations, Rigorous Epistemic Grounding, Unifying Semantic Understanding, Scope Transferability, and Targeted Prospective Validation. We present a start-to-finish case study of the iterative Random Forest (iRF) family under TRUST and contrast it with other LLM interpretation methods that struggle to clear specific tiers. Finally, we conclude with brief initial thoughts on how TRUST principles can extend in autonomous agentic frameworks. Ultimately, the TRUST framework fosters contestability and epistemic grounding as foundational evaluation principles for human-machine workflows and, eventually, autonomous agentic workflows.

papers.title: Contests versus Contracts in Innovation Procurement
papers.summary: How much competition should a designer introduce when procuring innovation? We study a designer funding multiple technological approaches whose feasibility is learned through experimentation. Between independent contracts and contests, we introduce interdependent contracts, which combine approach-specific rewards with continuation decisions that depend on rivals' outcomes. When both breakthroughs and breakdowns are contractable, these contracts implement the optimum by extracting firms' rents and coordinating experimentation across approaches. When only breakthroughs are contractable, we compare simple mechanisms with constant contractual payments. Under technological symmetry, optimal interdependent contracts terminate experimentation at a success cutoff or deadline. Fixed-prize contests can implement the same innovation outcomes, but their relative expenditure depends on the experimentation horizon: for interior success cutoffs, contests are more expensive when the horizon is short and less expensive when it is sufficiently long. Rank-contingent contests can weakly outperform constant-payment interdependent contracts, but technological heterogeneity can reverse this ranking because individualized contracts better tailor incentives to different approaches. We further characterize optimal interdependent contracts with time-varying payments, extending the comparison beyond simple mechanisms. Our results show how outcome contractability, technological heterogeneity, and payment flexibility shape the desirable form of competition in innovation procurement.

papers.title: Elastic polar oscillations and nuclear parameters
papers.summary: Owing to the elasticity of a neutron star, the shear and interface modes are excited, in addition to the fundamental, pressure, and gravity modes. While direct observations of the oscillation spectrum remain challenging, potential resonance signatures from these modes could be manifested in the precursors of short gamma-ray bursts from binary neutron star mergers. If the oscillation spectrum is observed, this is a good opportunity to extract the physical properties through the technique of asteroseismology. In particular, we focus on the crustal elasticity and examine the $s$- and $i$-mode frequencies. We find that, for a given EOS specified by the nuclear saturation parameters, the radius-scaled $s$-mode frequencies and the mass-scaled $i$-mode frequencies can be expressed as a function of the stellar compactness, independently of the stiffness of the core EOS, at least when the EOS in a higher-density region can be characterized only by the specific constant sound velocity. Then, we could derive the fitting formula for the $s_i$-mode for $i=1-4$ and $i_1$-mode frequencies as a function of the stellar compactness and the combination of the incompressibility of symmetric nuclear matter, $K_0$, and the slope parameter for the nuclear symmetry energy, $L$. If the $s$- and/or $i$-mode oscillation frequencies were observed, one may get the relation between these properties by identifying the observed frequencies with specific modes, using our fitting formula, which offers useful insights into the nuclear saturation parameters and stellar properties. By combining the other observational data, it may be possible to narrow the parameter space of EOS parameters and stellar properties. We emphasize that this article summarizes the results presented in our previous studies and discusses their implications for neutron star seismology.

papers.title: Lightest $Ω$-baryon systems with strangeness $-3$ and $-6$ within the framework of Faddeev and Faddeev--Yakubovsky equations
papers.summary: We investigate the binding energies and spatial properties of few-body $Ω$-baryon systems with strangeness $S=-3$ and $S=-6$ using the configuration-space Faddeev and Faddeev--Yakubovsky equations. For the first time, microscopic Faddeev--Yakubovsky calculations are performed for the four- and five-body $ΩNNN$, $ΩNNNN$, and $ΩΩNN$ systems. We employ HAL QCD and meson-exchange $ΩN$ interactions, together with the HAL QCD $ΩΩ$ potential, and examine the effects of Coulomb interactions and spin--isospin configurations. The calculations predict substantial enhancement of binding with increasing baryon number, with the most strongly bound $ΩNNNN$ configurations reaching approximately $60$~MeV and bound $ΩΩNN$ states in the $S=-6$ sector. The results reveal pronounced spin dependence and compact few-body structures, with the $Ω$ baryon preferentially localized near the center-of-mass. These findings provide new predictions for light multistrange nuclear systems and extend microscopic few-body calculations into the four- and five-body $Ω$-baryon sectors.

papers.title: Beyond the Thermodynamic-Volume Limit in Holographic Complexity
papers.summary: In the large black hole regime, holographic complexity obeys a thermodynamic-volume scaling law, while the finite-size approach to this limit remains unresolved. In this Letter, we develop an analytic description of finite-size corrections to this scaling for complexity of formation in the complexity=volume (CV) proposal of odd-dimensional equal-spinning Myers-Perry-AdS black holes. We find that the leading finite-size correction retains state dependence that is absent from the limiting thermodynamic-volume law. This correction changes sign at a distinguished Critical Horizon Ratio (CHR), where the generic leading finite-size contribution vanishes and convergence to the thermodynamic-volume law is correspondingly accelerated. We further determine the dimension dependence of the CHR analytically, showing that it approaches a finite nonextremal value at large dimension with a calculable leading finite-dimensional correction. These results show that the finite-size approach can provide a new probe of holographic structure, motivating its exploration across different realizations of holographic complexity and its eventual characterization in the dual field theory.

papers.title: A cubic theory of gravity with quasitopological-like properties for compactified cosmologies
papers.summary: We identify a cubic combination of curvature invariants in dimension $D=7$ that when added to the Einstein-Hilbert action, yields a healthy cosmological evolution in four dimensions after compactification on a constant-curvature internal space of dimension three. For generic backgrounds it leads to fourth-order field equations, nevertheless, on a warped product of a spatially flat, homogeneous and isotropic four-dimensional universe with a constant-curvature space of radius $b(t)$, the constraint is of first order in the scale factor $a(t)$ and in $b(t)$, while the remaining equations are of second order. Requiring this property uniquely singles out the cubic theory. We study the solutions describing a four-dimensional de Sitter Universe in direct product with an internal space of stabilized radius and evaluate its linear stability under time-dependent perturbations, showing that for a given sign of the curvature of the internal space, stability of the static solution fixes the sign of the higher curvature coupling. We also argue that linearized scalar perturbations depending on the spatial coordinates obey equations with at most two time derivatives. Finally, we numerically evolve the homogeneous and isotropic system non-linearly and present evidence that for a positive bare cosmological term $Λ_0$ and a hyperbolic compact space, the singularity formation present in GR in this ansatz is pushed into the future by increasing the higher-curvature coupling.

papers.title: Light-cone distributions of vector and scalar bound states in the Schwinger model from tensor networks
papers.summary: Light-cone distributions encode the partonic structure of hadrons, but they involve real-time correlations that Euclidean lattice methods cannot access directly. We compute the parton distribution functions (PDFs) and light-cone distribution amplitudes (LCDAs) of the vector and scalar meson bound states of the massive Schwinger model with tensor networks. Using the Kogut-Susskind lattice Hamiltonian with the gauge field eliminated through Gauss's law, we prepare the vacuum and the mesons as matrix product states and identify the vector and scalar mesons through their charge conjugation and momentum. The gauge-invariant light-cone correlators that define both distributions are evaluated directly in Minkowski space by real-time evolution. The two mesons exhibit qualitatively different light-cone structure, dictated by charge conjugation. The vector meson has a single-peaked PDF and a symmetric LCDA, while the scalar meson has a double-peaked PDF and an antisymmetric LCDA, whose vanishing zeroth moment requires a normalization through its first moment. The decay constants obtained from local matrix elements and from the moments of the LCDAs agree, and approach predictions from nonrelativistic model as the fermion mass increases. For the relatively large masses considered in this work, the PDFs closely follow the squared LCDAs, showing that the mesons are dominated by their valence component. Our results demonstrate tensor networks as a practical route to light-cone distributions of ground-state as well as excited hadrons in low-dimensional gauge theories.

papers.title: Where is the Interface for the AI Harness?
papers.summary: Norman's gulfs of execution and evaluation have guided interaction design for forty years, but both assume a user who is present in the loop. Agentic delegation breaks that assumption: users describe an outcome and leave, while the agent takes hundreds of unseen actions. Starting from a 2026 incident in which a research agent circumvented an access refusal on an Australian government portal and went unnoticed for two months, we argue that delegation opens two new gulfs. The gulf of specification is the gap between what a user wants and their ability to express it, including how the agent should behave in situations nobody foresaw. The gulf of oversight is the gap between what an agent is doing and the user's ability to know, assess, and control it. We argue that both gulfs meet in the harness, the tools, permissions, checks, and loop that surround the model. Harnesses are currently written by developers and hidden from users. We call on HCI to decide which parts of the harness belong to the end-user, which should be visible and adjustable defaults, and which should be built in by design, and to create the interfaces that let ordinary people author and read them.
papers.comment: Submitted and under review at Interaction

papers.title: BPS baryonic tubes in chiral perturbation theory minimally coupled with electrodynamics and a novel crossover
papers.summary: We derive a novel first-order BPS system (whose solutions are automatically solutions of the second-order field equations) in chiral perturbation theory (CPT) in $(3+1)$ dimensions. These BPS configurations describe baryonic tubes carrying a chiral current along the tubes themselves. Such baryonic tubes can be either homogeneous or modulated along the $z$-axis. We analyze the leading term in CPT, which is the $SU(2)$ non-linear sigma model minimally coupled to electrodynamics. These exact solutions are qualitatively different from the available analytic description of baryonic tubes since, due to their BPS nature, the positions of the energy-density peaks can be arbitrary. In contrast (in the case of the known solutions in the literature), the energy-density peaks' positions are fixed. We compare these two types of baryonic configurations; the relevant parameter that determines which one is energetically favored is the baryonic charge density: for low densities, the old solutions are favorable, while for high densities these novel BPS tubes are energetically favored. The inclusion of the electromagnetic field (together with the corresponding back-reaction on the baryonic tubes) can also be treated analytically. We discuss the differences in the electromagnetic field distribution between the two regions (low and high baryonic density). The analysis of potential terms for the chiral field is detailed in Appendix B.

papers.title: An entropy-adjusted invariant likelihood for incidental parameters
papers.summary: Incidental parameters can make maximum likelihood inconsistent in short panels. When they act through a known translation group, integration with respect to Haar measure eliminates them exactly and gives an invariant likelihood, whose score is shown to be the conditional expectation, given the maximal invariant, of the Neyman-orthogonalised score of every order. Under interactive fixed effects the orbit is an unknown factor space, and the invariant score for it has a drift equal to minus the derivative of the entropy of the retained contrasts. An entropy adjustment removes this drift and, at the true structural parameter, identifies the factor space uniquely when the loadings span it. The adjusted estimating equations are the gradient of a single criterion if and only if the entropy separates into an orbit term and an error-law term, as in scale and elliptical families; consistency then follows from a design condition, and in general from an equilibrium-identification condition, with asymptotic normality for fixed panel length. A boundary is derived for recovering a skewness sign discarded by a two-period invariant reduction. An application to Vietnamese rice farming rejects equal household-effect weights across survey waves and finds lower returns to scale.

papers.title: Rapid Exploratory Maps and their potential role in supporting evidence-to-policy dialogues and processes
papers.summary: Producing useful evidence syntheses requires clearly formulated research questions linked to an understanding of their optimal scope. When policymakers (or other end users) commission or steer the production of systematic reviews or other evidence syntheses to fulfil a demand for evidence, these parameters are rarely specified sufficiently for production to proceed. Instead, these details are typically developed via a collaborative dialogic process involving evidence producers and users to ensure the resulting synthesis will meet users' needs. This process is informed by scoping and (more-or-less formally) mapping the existing evidence base, which can take many weeks or months, slowed by applying mostly manual processes to identify and characterise the evidence. Recent developments in artificial intelligence (AI) technologies have opened up new opportunities for more rapid, iterative, and responsive mapping of relevant evidence to support such early-stage evidence-to-policy dialogues and processes. In this article, we outline and characterise this emerging approach, termed Rapid Exploratory Maps (REMs). We also present two illustrative case studies drawn from first-hand experiences within a programme of evidence reviews production to inform government policy in England. While this approach could be transformative for the mapping process, its broader potential is as yet largely unassessed, and it confers important challenges and likely risks, as well as benefits. Determining whether REMs could usefully support more efficient ways of working with end users when developing and designing evidence syntheses will require continued development and careful evaluation.

papers.title: The cyborg fly: reflexes survive engineered actuators, coordination needs stand-ins
papers.summary: Two wiring diagrams now cover the whole central nervous system of an adult fruit fly: one female, one male. Can such a diagram, run as a network of spiking neurons, drive a body? And if we swap the body's muscles for engineered actuators, what survives? We ran both connectomes, BANC and MaleCNS, as leaky integrate-and-fire networks of about 160,000 neurons each, and closed the loop through simulated sensors, actuators and bodies for walking and flight. The actuators are port-Hamiltonian, so energy is audited at every step, and swapping one for another changes only a configuration file. Null networks shuffled at five levels, from the whole nervous system to synapse counts, test whether a result depends on the wiring. The wiring produced specific functions: sugar on the labellum drove the proboscis motor neuron, leg joints resisted imposed movement, leg circuits oscillated, a looming disc drove a take-off signal on its side (in MaleCNS), and descending neurons throttled and steered flight. The resistance reflex survived 20 of 20 actuator settings in MaleCNS and 19 of 20 in BANC, including a Hill-type muscle pair and a geared DC motor; the actuator set walking speed and energy cost instead. Coordinated six-leg walking, flight stability and the correction of perturbations did not emerge. Each needed a labelled engineered stand-in, which the connectome could command. Such stand-ins can also manufacture an apparent dependence on wiring: in a rebuild of a published closed loop, odour navigation came from a hand-written rule, and the network entered only through one valence number. The two animals differed on some functions, and the differences traced to wiring, such as a haltere drive of the flight power muscles found only in MaleCNS. A whole-CNS connectome, embodied, gives reflexes, rhythms and command signals, but not the coordination that turns them into behaviour.
papers.comment: 27 pages, 7 figures. Submitted to PLOS Computational Biology. Code, configurations and figure data: Zenodo doi:10.5281/zenodo.24302416 (public on journal publication)

papers.title: The Self-Assembling Brain: Emergent Routing and Its Open Challenges
papers.summary: Biologically inspired alternatives to backpropagation, such as feedback alignment, relax the requirement for exact synaptic weight symmetry but still presuppose a fixed, pre-wired correspondence between forward and feedback pathways, an impasse Liao et al. (PNAS, 2026) term "architectural circularity." This commentary examines their Self-Assembling Motif (SAM), which reframes credit assignment as a self-organizing process driven by local synaptic rules. By linking ascending inference and descending feedback streams through initially random cross-stream connections, SAM supports local bridge alignment and emergent pathway alignment during stable training without fixed neuron-to-neuron pairing. Its resulting learning dynamics also exhibit adaptive preconditioning. The commentary highlights the algorithmic, biophysical, and temporal challenges that define the next research frontier: loss of neuron-specific nonlinear gating under straight-through approximation, compounding routing errors in deeper hierarchies, low-dimensional routing bottlenecks, the cortical implementation of non-driving modulatory connections, and the shift from alternating inference-update phases to continuous sensory processing.
papers.comment: PNAS Commentary on Liao et al. (2026)

papers.title: A source-based decomposition of thermal noise for mechanical system design
papers.summary: Thermal noise limits the sensitivity of precision mechanical instruments. We present a thermal- noise formulation for lumped-element mechanical systems that writes the total displacement thermal noise at the readout as the sum of contributions from all dissipative elements. For each contribution, we separate the thermal force generated by the element from its transfer to the readout. This decomposition provides simple design rules for comparing contributions from elements in series and in parallel and identifying the dominant noise source. It applies to frequency-dependent dissipation and to elements at different steady temperatures under local thermal equilibrium. We use it to identify the frequency regimes in which parallel and series dissipation dilution reduce displacement thermal noise. We then use examples of a pendulum on a lossy support, a rotational flexure, and rigidly mounted lunar optics to show how support noise can dominate even when the support has little effect on the system dynamics. Finally, a feedback-controlled suspension illustrates how sensing and actuation noise can be included in the same displacement-noise budget.

papers.title: A Kernel Framework for Linear Operator Equations
papers.summary: Solving linear operator equations with nonlocal terms or heterogeneous constraints often requires specific numerical schemes. We develop a unified approach based on embedding such equations into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). Differential, boundary, and integral operators are represented by their Riesz representers in the RKHS. The equations are solved in the regularized least-squares sense at finitely many collocation points. The solution is a finite linear combination of operator-induced representers and is obtained from a single linear system. Its sensitivities, such as financial Greeks, follow by direct differentiation. To reduce the computational cost for large collocation sets, we introduce a Nyström approximation based on subsampling the operator-induced representers. It yields the best approximation of this solution within the reduced trial space, in a regularized empirical norm. Numerical examples cover ordinary, partial, and partial integro-differential equations, including multi-asset and jump-diffusion option pricing.

papers.title: Training decision models for simulating human respondents
papers.summary: Researchers increasingly use large language models (LLMs) as synthetic respondents in market research, conjoint analysis, and randomized experiments. However, synthetic choice data from off-the-shelf generative LLMs bias downstream econometric inference. Neither proprietary models nor higher reasoning effort reliably reduces this bias. We investigate decision models (System One architectures) for silicon sampling. Using choice training, we update KEV model weights on historical respondent-level choice microdata by conditional maximum likelihood, before inference and without target-study data. Across three model scales, training on two discrete choice experiments lowers treatment-effect error by 22% to 89% on four held-out studies from new domains (vaccines, nutrition labels, consumer rights, and AI) and new response formats. A small choice-trained model outperforms a much larger off-the-shelf model on three of the four studies. Although training on single studies lowers cross-entropy, it can exacerbate treatment-effect error. Choice training thus complements post-inference calibration by providing a stronger starting point for estimating human preferences.

papers.title: Latent Channel Completion for Forecasting in Sensor Networks with Failed Detectors
papers.summary: Monitoring networks for traffic and utility infrastructure lose sensors routinely, and forecasting models that couple sensors together to gain accuracy also inherit an exposure to those losses. When a detector stops reporting, the substituted value is embedded as though it were a reading and propagates through the shared representation that couples the network, degrading forecasts for sensors that are still healthy. Because these models are selected on benchmarks where every sensor reports, the exposure is absent from the numbers used to choose them. We introduce Latent Channel Completion, a channel-axis joint embedding predictive objective that reconstructs missing sensors' latent representations rather than their values, since a coupling operator consumes embeddings and never sees raw readings. Channels are masked during training and their representations predicted from surviving channels against stop-gradient targets; at inference the operator fills in whichever sensors the monitoring system reports as dark, using parameters shared with the forecaster. On three highway detector networks, after half of each network goes dark, the accuracy advantage of coupling changes by -1.0, -0.5 and +8.8 percentage points, against losses of 10.2 to 50.3 points for the unmodified forecaster, which on one network falls behind an uncoupled reference entirely. Against cross-channel ridge imputation drawing on the same surviving sensors, completing the latent lowers error by a further 13.9% and 28.6%, and on complete inputs, the method matches its backbone. The benefit tracks how much a network gains from coupling when intact, giving operators a criterion evaluable before any outage occurs.

papers.title: The Paradox of Agency-Preserving AI: Negotiating Learner Agency in Layered Human-AI Interactions
papers.summary: Generative AI is increasingly used by learners in cognitively demanding tasks, but its capacity to provide immediate solutions raises concerns about decreased learner agency. Meta-level AI systems that provide reflective and metacognitive scaffolding have emerged as a promising approach to supporting learners' self-regulation. However, these systems introduce a fundamental paradox: AI intended to preserve learner agency can itself constrain that agency by regulating when, how, and why learners should reflect. To investigate this challenge, we conducted a co-design workshop with 18 students engaged in programming and academic writing tasks using ChatGPT extended with ChatWise, a meta-level AI system providing self-regulated learning-aligned feedback. Drawing on 185 prompt-feedback entries, 174 written reflections, and participants' design artifacts (17 storyboards and 5 group design proposals), we identified four interconnected design tensions: assistance vs reflection, immediate intervention vs space for self-regulation, visibility vs attention competition, and system adaptation vs user control. The study contributes a multidimensional account of learner agency that includes task, cognitive, and interaction agency, along with empirically grounded interaction-design mechanisms to negotiate these tensions.

papers.title: COGENT: A Modular Cognitive Architecture for Agentic User Simulation
papers.summary: LLM-based user simulation can support interface design, accessibility research, and interactive-agent evaluation, but standard computer-use agents are optimized for task completion rather than reproducing how people perceive, reason, and act. We introduce COGENT (COGnitive agENT), a modular cognitive architecture for simulating user interaction with desktop interfaces. COGENT draws on established cognitive theories, such as Norman's action cycle and ACT-R, to enable explainable, intervenable, and modular user simulation by decomposing the simulation process into cognitive modules with explicit representations of perception, memory, user state, intentions, and action selection. We begin by presenting six intervenability demonstrations, each tracing how a single edit to memory, a user attribute, or a processing module propagates through the cognitive pipeline to produce a behavioral change. We evaluate COGENT's behavioral and attributional fidelity across three benchmarks -- AgentNetBench, A11y-CUA, and SENSE-42 -- finding that it achieves statistically significant fidelity gains over computer-use baselines in reproducing recorded human behavior and recovers the relational structure among human self-reported psychological states. Together, these demos and evaluations demonstrate COGENT's utility toward more faithful, explainable, intervenable, and modular LLM-based cognitive simulations.

papers.title: Fairness and incentives in combinatorial assignment
papers.summary: We consider the fair and efficient random assignment of indivisible goods subject to resource constraints. Agents receive bundles randomly, but individual lotteries over bundles that are feasible in expectation need not be jointly feasible. Consequently, we treat a lottery over feasible allocations as a public good. We show that every feasible finite economy admits an envy-free and Pareto efficient random assignment that may be supported as a Lindahl equilibrium. For a finite type space with specified expected utilities, we construct a mechanism whose outcomes are exactly feasible and Pareto efficient with respect to reported preferences. As the population grows and empirical type proportions and per-capita resources approach a limiting large economy, envy and gains from manipulation vanish. The approximate incentive compatibility of the mechanism holds for all type profiles that approximate the limiting economy. The argument combines sensitivity bounds for linear programs with proximity bounds between fractional and integer optima.

papers.title: Tempering and few-shot calibration of pathology foundation models improve digital biomarker reproducibility across slide scanners
papers.summary: Pathology foundation models underpin a growing number of histology-based cancer biomarkers, but sensitivity to slide scanner-specific image signatures degrades cross-center reliability and reproducibility. We developed a foundation model fine-tuning method that improved consistency in head-and-neck cancer human papillomavirus (HPV) prediction, colorectal cancer microsatellite instability (MSI) identification, prostate cancer grading and breast cancer phenotyping. This tempering method decreased cross-scanner prediction differences by 67.5% for HPV (95% CI 59.0-73.9%), 69.3% for MSI (95% CI 51.9-76.5%) and 63.4%-81.2% for breast signatures. Cross-scanner prostate grade agreement rose from 42.5% to 92.7%. Under full scanner-HPV confounding during training, AUROC fell from 0.80 to 0.68 with original model features but only from 0.86 to 0.84 with tempering. Unlike post hoc feature calibration, tempering used only public data yet matched or exceeded on-site calibration. These findings support tempering to reduce scanner dependence of pathology foundation models.

papers.title: Can LLM-Simulated Respondents Pre-Test Survey Questions? Evidence From Preregistered Prospective Validation
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can be conditioned to simulate behavioral responses, including survey responses, but it remains unclear whether and how these simulations can support downstream research tasks. Here, we evaluate whether simulated respondents can support pre-testing new candidate survey questions before fielding them, operationalized as prioritizing candidate survey items. Specifically, we rank candidate questions by their mean responses, which can reveal ceiling or floor effects; their variance, which indicates whether responses contain meaningful variation; and differences between subpopulations, which indicate whether questions capture distinctions between relevant groups within a population. We introduce a preregistered, prospective evaluation that commits model predictions before target human responses exist, ruling out memorization of those responses by design. Using two waves of a local survey (2025: N = 1,271; 2026: N = 1,161), we built simulated respondents from 2025 participants and preregistered GPT-4.1 predictions for 22 questions introduced in 2026. Simulations accurately ranked questions by mean responses (Spearman \r{ho} = 0.71) and anticipated which questions distinguished city from county residents (\r{ho} = 0.88), Black from White residents (\r{ho} = 0.68), and employed from unemployed residents (\r{ho} = 0.57), suggesting simulations can help prioritize questions before fielding. More broadly, our prospective, preregistered design provides a general framework for evaluating AI simulations without contamination from memorized target outcomes.

papers.title: Burning the Bridge: Agentification and Domestic Value Added
papers.summary: Firms that replace local work with foreign AI agents can produce more per paid hour while generating less income at home. We study this trade-off in a small open economy where exporters and local services both use agents. Once wages reach a reservation floor, extending agent use in local services lowers domestic income at unchanged foreign costs. Value added at constant prices and consumption also fall if suppliers capture enough of the saving. Exporters have an offset: adopting agents can expand production and earn the foreign exchange needed to pay for them. The difference is substantial. Using Brazilian accounts as a reference, a supplier bargaining share above about 0.15 is sufficient to make further local-service adoption reduce value added even at negligible foreign costs. The corresponding threshold in tradables is about 0.66. We derive separate export-growth requirements for preserving income and consumption and illustrate them using historical accounts for Brazil and Mexico. Cheaper agents ease the consumption requirement; lower export prices raise it. Over time, declining domestic capabilities can also make returning to local production more expensive, allowing suppliers to charge more at renewal.

papers.title: Pretrained Tabular Features and the Measurement of Financial Proximity
papers.summary: Spatial arbitrage pricing theory (S-APT) extends factor models to allow returns to spill over between connected firms, beyond what common risk factors explain. In recent years, tabular foundation models (TFMs) have matched or outperformed tuned gradient-boosted and bagged ensembles on small and medium-sized tabular benchmarks. Although their predictive performance is strong, these models reveal little about what they have learned, which limits their use in regulated financial applications that require explanation. Internal representations are widely used to probe what neural networks learn and to measure similarity. In this paper, we use the frozen representations of four TFMs as a measure of financial dissimilarity in a spatial asset-pricing model of US equities from 2011 to 2025, and find that their estimated gains over a direct distance between the same disclosures become consistently positive once broad SEC filing data are included. This reframes tabular foundation models from black-box predictors into instruments for measuring economic structure, with immediate applications to peer selection, risk attribution and network-based asset pricing. More broadly, our findings suggest that the internal representations of foundation models, not only their predictions, deserve study as economic objects, opening a new line of research on what pretrained models know about firms.

papers.title: CRAB-H: Task-Centric Certification for Healthcare Autonomous Systems
papers.summary: This paper introduces CRAB H as a task-centric certification methodology for healthcare autonomous systems. CRAB H extends the ARC governance architecture by introducing the task as a first-class governance object, represented through Task Requirement Profiles TRP H. Each profile defines the cognitive capabilities, governance constraints, evidentiary requirements, and operational assumptions necessary for the safe execution of a specific healthcare activity. Rather than asking whether a robot achieves a sufficiently high benchmark score, CRAB H asks whether demonstrated capabilities satisfy the requirements of the task. Certification becomes a comparison between demonstrated capability and required capability. A reliability-gated assurance allocation mechanism routes cognitive dimensions that cannot be reproducibly evaluated to LEA operational requirements rather than discarding them. Governance integrity is preserved: unreliable dimensions are governed, not ignored. The Capability Margin is defined as the threshold-based conjunction of per-dimension compliance determinations, not as a subtracted scalar preserving non compensatory governance logic appropriate for safety-critical healthcare deployment

papers.title: Symbolic Proof Compression and Fractal Universality: A Conditional Non-Constructive Refutation of the Riemann Hypothesis
papers.summary: Building on S.~C.~Woon's (1994) fractal and symbolic reformulation of Voronin's Universality Theorem, we construct a formal, non-constructive proof-by-contradiction architecture exploring the Riemann Hypothesis ($\mathsf{RH}$). Woon's Corollary~3 permits arbitrary finite binary strings to be encoded into nowhere-vanishing exponential waveforms on a closed disk inside the critical strip. Combining effective upper bounds for Voronin universality (Good, Garunkštis) with Cauchy-integral Taylor decoding yields an explicit finite rational grid $\mathcal{G}_{L_0}$ below an effective ceiling $H_{\mathrm{crit}}(L_0)$ within which every formal proof of bit-length at most $L_0$ is imprinted with zero flipped digits. We introduce a conjectural \emph{Zeta-Universal Symbolic Proof Compression Hypothesis} ($\mathsf{SPC}_{\mathsf{RH}}$), positing that the global regularity implied by $\mathsf{RH}$ compresses true $Π_1^0$ statements about $ζ(s)$ into $\mathsf{ZFC}$ derivations of bounded length $L_0$. Assuming classical logic and $\mathsf{SPC}_{\mathsf{RH}}$, Gödel--Carnap diagonalization over bounded zeta-encoded provability yields a contradiction. The self-referential result converts a digital encoding framework with any uniform proof-compression principle for RH into an immediate non-constructive refutation of RH. Given that, with human input and computer assistance, $\mathsf{RH}$ has been formally verified in the Lean theorem prover strictly within constructive logic, this contradiction does not refute $\mathsf{RH}$. Instead, it falsifies $\mathsf{SPC}_{\mathsf{RH}}$. We conclude by isolating the exact proof-theoretic obstruction---Pudlák's lower bound on bounded reflection proofs---showing why the analytic regularity of $\mathsf{RH}$ cannot compress logical self-reference, and exposing the limits of applying the Law of Excluded Middle to uncomputably bounded searches.

papers.title: Anisotropic Fluid Inhomogeneous Cosmology
papers.summary: We propose a new framework for inhomogeneous cosmology based on General Relativity sourced by an anisotropic fluid. The model is parametrized by a single input function, the radial Misner--Sharp mass distribution at different redshifts, and admits exact solutions to Einstein's equations. Going beyond the standard assumption of small metric perturbations, it provides a fully relativistic framework to describe the non-linear regime of cosmic structure formation. The Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) cosmology is recovered both at early times and -- on large scales only -- at late times. Our Anisotropic Fluid Inhomogeneous Cosmology (AFIC) model provides a natural mechanism through which matter inhomogeneities give rise to late-time acceleration. The extensive term driving this effect does not enter the exact metric solution and therefore does not contribute to the local gravitational potential. Rather, it emerges as a genuinely large-scale effect induced by the inhomogeneous distribution of matter at late times. This mechanism may provide a physical interpretation of the results from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI). Finally, we present a simple analytical realization of the model and use it to provide an estimate of the present-day effective dark energy density.
papers.comment: 15 pages, no figures, comments are welcome

papers.title: The Relaxation of Quantum Near-Extremal Black Holes. (I) Microcanonical States, Pruning of Quasinormal Modes, and the Aretakis Instability
papers.summary: The late-time relaxation of a near-extremal black hole is classically governed by an infinite tower of purely damped quasinormal modes. This poses a puzzle: the higher overtones decay at rates much larger than the energy $E$ of the black hole above extremality, so they would need black hole states below the extremal mass. We resolve it by including the quantum fluctuations that become large when $E$ falls below a scale $E_b$. We compute the retarded Green's function of a probe of conformal dimension $Δ$ in a black hole of fixed energy, and find that each classical mode splits into a pair of poles with real parts set by $E_b$. The perturbed black hole decays as an unstable quantum system, and a pair is a resonance, i.e., a quasinormal mode, only if its energy lies within the accessible black hole spectrum. This prunes the tower to finitely many modes, all damped faster than $Δ^2E_b$, and below $E=Δ^2E_b/2$ none is left. For generic $Δ$, the response of the black hole decays first as $t^{-2Δ}$ and finally as $t^{-3/2}$, with an exponential stage in between if $E\ggΔ^2E_b$. The same quantum effects bear on the Aretakis instability of extremal black holes, in which transverse derivatives of a perturbation grow without bound on the horizon. Like the tower of modes, it originates in the scale invariance of the classical throat, which the quantum fluctuations break. The $t^{-2Δ}$ decay, which is the boundary counterpart of the Aretakis growth, ends by $t\sim1/E_b$, when the throat ceases to be classical, and by then horizon derivatives have grown only to a finite value. Their unbounded growth is an artifact of taking the semiclassical limit before the late-time one, two limits that in quantum mechanics do not commute.

papers.title: Gluon GPDs from hard-exclusive electroproduction of heavy quarkonium at NLO
papers.summary: Gluon tomography of the nucleon through hard-exclusive electroproduction of $J/ψ$ has been one of the key motivations for Electron-Ion Collider. However, the next-to-leading order (NLO) perturbative QCD calculations available in the literature were performed either in the collinear factorization limit where the heavy-quark mass is neglected, or in heavy-quark limit where the heavy quarkonia are approximately point-like. We present a full next-to-leading order collinear factorization for the hard exclusive production of heavy mesons that retains the meson mass as well as full light-cone distribution amplitude. We compare the full NLO result with the special limits and estimate the errors due to potentially-large corrections from $α_s(M)$ and $M^2/Q^2$ at this order.

papers.title: A multimodal foundation model for tissue proteomics and morphology in cancer
papers.summary: Cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment decisions increasingly rely on integrating tissue morphology with specific molecular readouts of the tumor and its microenvironment. H&E histopathology provides scalable morphology, whereas multiplex spatial proteomics quantifies dozens of proteins in situ with spatial context, but remains selectively deployed, often with different marker panels across cohorts. This creates a translational bottleneck: most patients lack high-depth molecular profiling, and existing models rarely integrate morphology and spatial molecular data in a single framework. We present VirTues-M2, a multimodal foundation model that jointly learns from H&E and spatial proteomics using a novel vision transformer-based architecture. By encoding marker identity during pretraining, VirTues-M2 is robust to missing modalities, imperfect modality pairing or registration, and variable marker panels, enabling unified inference for tissue phenotyping, panoptic cell segmentation, virtual staining, annotation-free biomarker discovery, and reinforcement learning-based adaptive marker panel selection to reduce assay burden. As a concrete demonstration of translational utility, in a newly collected cohort of 1,053 treatment-naive non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients with paired spatial proteomics and H&E, VirTues-M2 discovers high-risk and low-risk tissue signatures that stratify overall survival in both the discovery cohort and an independent validation cohort, outperforming current state-of-the-art stratification schemes; all enabled by VirTues-M2's ability to jointly analyze both modalities within a single model.

papers.title: Split Ends: UV Physics branches Black Hole Hair
papers.summary: Coupling a shift-symmetric scalar field to the Gauss-Bonnet invariant modifies black holes (BHs) via scalar hair. Here we consider this field to be the Goldstone of a complex scalar field with a symmetry-breaking potential. For BHs of a size comparable with the inverse mass gap, the gapped field tries to restore the symmetry close to the horizon, enhancing the departure from standard BHs. Moreover, BHs of the same mass can have up to three different horizon areas and surface gravities. This branching has profound consequences for BH physics, potentially observable in gravitational waves.

papers.title: Nuclear deep-inelastic scattering as a BSM probe via SMEFT
papers.summary: Searches for New Physics at the energy frontier have motivated theoretical development of model-independent methods to constrain interactions beyond the Standard Model (BSM) like the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT), as well as associated phenomenological analyses. While these approaches are powerful, they are also afflicted by the large space of higher-dimensional operators and the challenge of possible degeneracies among these operators. To help ameliorate these difficulties, processes beyond those at hadron colliders, including deep-inelastic scattering (DIS), have been identified and studied for their ability to contribute added constraining power. In this work, we extend such investigations to charged-lepton DIS involving heavy nuclei, for which we explore the systematics of SMEFT effects for a series of representative cases. In particular, we point out that nuclear effects can reshuffle the luminosities governing partons entering SMEFT-corrected hard interactions, such that the nucleus can serve as an expanded laboratory to explore SMEFT effects complementary to free-nucleon DIS. In particular, we find that nuclear DIS possesses significant constraining power over flavor-isovector SMEFT operator combinations, with reduced nPDF dependence; similarly, improved control over nPDFs would further enhance the SMEFT reach of nuclear DIS observables. We explore projections for future (proposed) facilities like the EIC, LHeC, and FCC-eh, finding that improvements to nuclear parton distribution functions (nPDFs) can further sharpen the reach of nuclear DIS.

papers.title: Quantum black hole evaporation from thin shell collapse: a complete effective picture
papers.summary: Quantum gravity is expected to play a central role in resolving classical singularities and providing a complete, predictive spacetime picture. In this paper, we develop an effective model inspired by loop quantum gravity that aims to fulfill this expectation, providing a unified description of thin shell collapse, black hole formation, evaporation, and remnant dynamics. The framework exhibits general validity, holding across different effective equations of motion, matter sources, and evaporation laws. Specifically, we incorporate backreaction within a quasi-static approximation, modeling the radiation as null dust and matching the ingoing and outgoing fluxes across an evaporation surface using the Darmois-Israel junction conditions. For an evaporation law governed by the Stefan-Boltzmann law, we find that the final stage of evaporation yields an extremal black hole extending into a new asymptotic region, featuring both event and Cauchy horizons. Conversely, under the Schwinger approach, no event or Cauchy horizons form, instead, a temporary dynamical trapped region emerges, and the resulting spacetime remains globally hyperbolic. Under this variant, our model predicts a horizonless null remnant escaping to future null infinity.

papers.title: Refined Rényi Entropy from Replica-Geometry Tensor Networks
papers.summary: Holographic tensor networks are a central route to understanding the mechanism behind the holographic duality, but standard fixed-graph constructions with maximally entangled links face a structural obstacle. Their leading entanglement spectra are flat, so their Rényi entropies do not depend on the replica index. This is in sharp contrast with holographic conformal field theories, where a tensionful cosmic brane makes the refined Rényi entropy $n$-dependent. Capturing this replica dependence is therefore an important test of tensor-network descriptions of holographic entanglement. We construct an explicit family of replica-dependent geodesic graphs that reproduces this behavior while keeping the links maximally entangled. For each replica index $n$, geodesics are emitted from the replicated boundary with the same local, isotropic intersection measure. They perfectly tessellate the selected replica geometry, so the $n$-dependence of their intersection counts comes from the geometry. Tensor-network models on these graphs reproduce the cosmic-brane prescription for refined Rényi entropy by counting crossing threads. Their cross-copy endpoint density also agrees, in CFT$_2$, with a boundary reconstruction within the additive linear combination proposal, providing a check beyond the total entropy. In higher dimensions, we further obtain an analytic large-separation decay law for this density.

papers.title: How Far Can Linear Go? BiPert, a Unified Framework for Single-Cell Perturbation Modelling
papers.summary: Understanding how genetic perturbations affect cellular behaviour is essential for studying gene function and regulatory mechanisms. Large-scale CRISPR screens measure these effects across thousands of genes, but cover relatively few cellular contexts. Predicting perturbation responses in unseen cell types and identifying perturbed genes from their transcriptional effects therefore remain challenging. Here, we show that both tasks can be addressed through a common linear decomposition of transcriptional responses into shared and perturbation-specific components. Building on this principle, we introduce BiPert, a simple linear framework for both forward perturbation prediction and inverse identification. For forward prediction, BiPert outperforms existing methods that use no external biological knowledge when predicting gene expression changes in unseen cell lines. Its few-shot extension, BiPert-FS, adapts to new cell lines using as few as ten measured perturbations. For inverse identification, BiPert-ID identifies perturbed genes from single-cell expression profiles, outperforming deep-learning methods in unseen cell lines and donors. We further show that perturbations whose effects transfer more consistently across cellular contexts are also easier to identify, even after controlling for perturbation effect size. Together, these results establish a connection between perturbation transfer and identification, and demonstrate that simple linear models provide strong, interpretable baselines for both tasks.

papers.title: A Mixed-Methods Study of Personal Software Creation
papers.summary: People have long wanted software shaped around their own data, routines, and preferences. We refer to such software as \emph{personal software}. For decades, programming expertise limited who could build it: people without that expertise could build software only within constrained end-user programming tools, such as spreadsheets. AI coding agents seem to remove this bottleneck by letting people build full applications from natural-language descriptions, and many people now build and share personal software publicly. Yet personal software has rarely been studied at scale: we know little about what people build and why, how they build it, and what opportunities and challenges they encounter. We investigate these questions with a mixed-methods study. A grey-literature review examines 6,168 web and Reddit posts, and an observation study follows eight people as they build software for their own needs with AI coding agents and use it for up to a week. We find that creators value personal software for how closely it fits a particular person or community. The software takes shape as creators react to what the agent builds: most functionality emerged during building, and creators' effort shifted from writing code to checking it.

papers.title: Know When to Abstain: Conformal Confidence Estimation for Text-to-SQL
papers.summary: Text-to-SQL systems often return queries that execute successfully but answer the wrong question. Detecting these errors at deployment is hard because execution correctness is defined against a gold query, which exists only in labeled data. We formulate confidence estimation for Text-to-SQL as probabilistic query validation under a latent correctness variable that is observable at calibration time through gold-SQL execution and latent at deployment. Our estimator separates generation from validation. A generator LLM writes and executes the query, and a different critic LLM judges the query and its execution result. The critic's validation and execution-grounded alignment scores are fused with the generator's verbalized confidence, token-level uncertainty, and SQL-structural features in a Random Forest, using two sequential LLM calls. Two calibration steps give finite-sample guarantees. A Learn-then-Test threshold ensures, with probability $1-δ$, that the error rate among accepted queries stays below a user-chosen budget. A conformal p-value bounds the false abstention rate. On Spider we use GPT-OSS-120B as generator and Gemma-4-31B as critic. The estimator obtains an AUARC of 0.899. Without abstention, 22.6% of queries are wrong. With a 15% risk budget ($δ=0.1$), a threshold is certified on all 10 resampled splits, and the system accepts 52.4% of queries on average with 9.1% observed error. Five different critic models give similar results. In a controlled comparison on Spider with Olmo-3-32B as generator, the estimator obtains an AUARC of 89.5, compared with 81.2 for the strongest logit-based baseline. Applied to BIRD without retraining, the confidence scores remain informative (AUROC 0.72, against 0.79 on Spider), but the risk guarantee does not transfer, as expected without exchangeability.

papers.title: Emulator-enabled calibration and uncertainty quantification of $β$-decay calculations within the energy density functional theory
papers.summary: Predictions of $β$-decay half-lives of neutron-rich nuclei and their uncertainties critically impact our understanding of the astrophysical rapid neutron capture process. To provide quantified predictions within nuclear energy density functional theory, as customarily done, we perform Bayesian calibrations of two coupling constants: the isoscalar proton-neutron pairing strength and the isovector spin-density coupling. We apply an E-optimal experimental design for choosing the calibration sets. We employ the proton-neutron finite-amplitude method with Skyrme energy density functionals using emulators of half-lives and Gamow--Teller resonance energies. The calculated $Q_β$ values are fine-tuned to experimental values. The contributions to the half-life uncertainty from the theory error, $Q_β$ values, and the parameter uncertainty are all accounted for in the Bayesian framework. Our predictions for the even-even $N=126$ isotones provide the shortest half-lives for neutron-rich nuclei among the existing theoretical models, which would affect the flow of heavy-element nucleosynthesis. The proposed framework allows quantified theoretical uncertainties to be propagated to astrophysical observables such as abundance patterns and electromagnetic emission.

papers.title: Place-Based Policy from Space: Evidence from Italy's Inner Areas
papers.summary: This paper evaluates a place-based policy, Italy's National Strategy for Inner Areas (SNAI), using satellite nighttime lights. Targeting structurally fragile and peripheral municipalities, SNAI invests in essential services and economic activities. Staggered difference-in-differences compares 941 funded municipalities with 3,112 eligible controls over 2011--2022. Funding is associated with an expansion of lit area and no detectable change in radiance per lit cell, suggesting that activity extends its footprint rather than intensifying in existing centres. The expansion holds across comparison groups and, descriptively, concentrates at intermediate funding per resident. Annual satellite data can complement slower and coarser statistics.

papers.title: Tradeoffs between objective outcomes and human enjoyment of work in human-AI task allocation
papers.summary: For people, tasks at work are defined by more than their outcome: they are colored by the experience of engaging in that task.
